questions.q: List the two main supporting characters in "The Adventure of the Three Garridebs" and state their stated professions/identities when first introduced.
questions.a: The two main supporting characters are John Garrideb (introduced as a Counsellor at Law from Kansas, USA) and Nathan Garrideb (introduced as a collector/scholar living at 136 Little Ryder Street). A wrong answer (e.g., naming Holmes or Watson, or missing one) reveals the student cannot distinguish protagonists from supporting characters or has not tracked the character introductions in the narrative sequence.

questions.q: Explain the difference between John Garrideb's stated motive for finding a third Garrideb and his actual motive, using one piece of textual evidence for each.
questions.a: Stated motive: John claims he needs a third Garrideb to inherit Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's $15 million estate (five million each), as per the will's condition. Evidence: "It's five million dollars for each if it is a cent, but we can't lay a finger on it until we all three stand in a row." Actual motive: He needs Nathan Garrideb out of his rooms at 136 Little Ryder Street to access the counterfeiting press hidden beneath the floorboards by previous tenant Rodger Presbury. Evidence: Holmes discovers "a printing press—a counterfeiter's outfit" in the cellar after John pries up the floorboards. A wrong answer that only states the surface motive shows the student accepts character dialogue at face value without analyzing dramatic irony or Holmes's deduction.

questions.q: Using the STEAL method (Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks), complete a character trait chart for Nathan Garrideb with one textual example for each element.
questions.a: S (Speech): "Syracusan—of the best period... They degenerated greatly towards the end." Shows scholarly obsession. T (Thoughts): "Why should I go out when I have so much to hold me here?" Reveals reclusive contentment. E (Effect): Holmes treats him with "personal touch" and kindness; John Garrideb exploits his "queer name." A (Actions): Polishing coins, cataloguing cabinets, agreeing to Birmingham trip reluctantly. L (Looks): "Cadaverous face," "large round spectacles," "goat's beard," "stooping attitude." A wrong answer that invents traits not in the text (e.g., "greedy" or "suspicious") reveals the student projects protagonist-like agency onto a passive victim character.

questions.q: Analyze how John Garrideb and Nathan Garrideb function as character foils to each other. Provide three specific contrasts with textual support.
questions.a: 1. Physicality: John is "short, powerful," "chubby," "round, fresh clean-shaven face"; Nathan is "very tall, loose jointed, round-backed," "gaunt and bald," "cadaverous face." 2. Mobility: John is an active predator who "burst excitedly into the room," travels from America, plans the Birmingham trip; Nathan is sedentary: "I very seldom leave my room," needs persuasion to travel. 3. Motivation: John pursues criminal gain (counterfeiting plates) through elaborate deception; Nathan pursues knowledge (collection) through genuine scholarship. A wrong answer that only lists differences without the "foil" concept (how each highlights the other's traits) shows superficial comparison without literary analysis.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of John Garrideb's disguise as an American lawyer. Why does Holmes see through it immediately, and what does this reveal about the criminal's limitations?
questions.a: The disguise fails because of inconsistent details: English coat "frayed at the elbow," trousers "bagged at the knee with a year's wear," yet he claims recent arrival from America. Holmes notes: "Touch him where you would he was false." The advertisement for "Howard Garrideb" uses American spellings ("plow," "buckboards," "artesian wells") purporting to be from an English firm. This reveals John Garrideb/Killer Evans, despite his "devilish ingenuity" in constructing the Garrideb narrative, lacks Holmes's attention to minutiae—the very skill that defines the detective. A wrong answer that says "Holmes is just smarter" misses the textual evidence of specific physical and linguistic clues that the criminal overlooked.

questions.q: Create a diary entry from Nathan Garrideb's perspective on the evening after the arrest, expressing his realization about the "three Garridebs" and his lost dreams. Use at least three textual phrases from the story.
questions.a: A strong entry captures his voice (scholarly, innocent, devastated) and incorporates phrases like "dissipated dreams," "castle in the air fell down," "rigmarole of lies," or "glory of hope." It should show his delayed understanding that the inheritance was fiction and his collection—the "nucleus of a national collection"—remains unpurchased. A poor entry makes him sound angry or detective-like rather than heartbroken and bewildered, revealing the student hasn't internalized his passive, eccentric characterization.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of supporting characters involves examining their personality traits, motivations, narrative functions, and ______ to the protagonist and plot, using textual evidence to explain how they advance themes, create conflict, or serve as foils in a literary work.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a criminal profiler trying to ______ why a seemingly harmless collector was targeted by a master criminal.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured, evidence-based character sketch of both John Garrideb (Killer Evans) and Nathan Garrideb, explaining their contrasting roles as antagonist and victim, analyzing how their characterization drives the plot's central deception, and evaluating their function as foils to Holmes and Watson.
